poiARC-desc:
The American Reclamation Corporation did not set out to {{poiARC003|become a power}}. It began as a contractor, hired by a failing government to do what the government could no longer do: pull survivors out of the flooded coasts, feed them, and {{poiARC002|put them somewhere safe}}. Every disaster that followed the Great Mistake was another contract, and every contract was done a little better than the last. By the time Central noticed what had happened, the people in the camps knew whose name was on the ration crates.

Today ARC is less a company than a state that happens to file quarterly reports. {{poiARC005|Its divisions}} handle everything a government would: peace, security, food, medicine, energy, logistics, and human resources. Where ARC governs, it does so through oversight boards, research mandates and checkpoints, and its subjects are treated as customers first and citizens second. Its prices are fair, its service is reliable, and it never forgets a debt.

The Corporation's great promise is {{poiARC004|rejuvenation}}, the research that has made its Chief Research Officer a feared name and its Vice Presidents the envy of the Districts. For most people, longer life is the only argument ARC needs. Critics warn that a company that {{poiARC001|sells time}} holds a lever no government ever had. ARC answers that it has never asked anyone to believe in it, only to look at who is still standing.

Its rivals are Central, which still holds the Union's seat but not its loyalty, and any District that has begun to ask whether the contract can be cancelled. ARC has never needed to answer that question with force. It prefers to let the checkpoints, the water and the rations do it.
poiARC001-desc:
In a world where the clock seems to tick ever closer against humanity, where so many are dying to famine, disease, poverty and violence, you would think that the seemingly imminent doom would force everybody to either come to grips with the ramifications, or go mad from the weight of it. ARC CEO Michael Moderski is one of the few who is completely immunized from this psychological phenomenon, acting no differently than if he was born at the height of human society just prior to the Great Mistake.

Having formed the American Reclamation Corporation from the 2170s to 2180s, through a process of systematically merging privatized District industries, Moderski only has one personal goal for himself—to live well, and to make sure he has to work as little as possible to do so. With him effectively handing control of basically every major company operation to Chief Financial Officer Suzanne Fielding, Moderski is spending most of his time trying to ensure his ludicrously high personal wealth keeps increasing, and to spend it on the handful of luxury items still available to purchase. He is confident that the gravy train will keep rolling into the station for as long as he is CEO of the ARC.
poiARC002-desc: Arcopolis is an anthill of humanity, the beacon of the East. Millions call the shore city their home. It teems with factory workers, scientists, merchants and foreign delegates. Arcopolis is not just a corporate headquarters, but has morphed itself into the continent's biggest city.
poiARC003-desc:
One of the means by which the American Reclamation Corporation got to where it is today was sheer ambition. An unquenchable drive to do more, to be more, to help America, and to help the world.

The founding virtues of ARC are integrity, practicality, and trust. ARC aims to expand its scope across the globe and partner with as many nations as possible. ARC believes that only by working together can real progress be achieved.

Please call 3924-192 for more information or contact your nearest ARC delegation for more information on how you, your community, or your country can initiate profitable dealings with ARC.
poiARC004-desc:
ARC's most ambitious research does not happen in Arcopolis. It happens in District 8, in old Canada, where ARC R&D runs extensive facilities for engineering, AI design and every other field that needs heavy infrastructure. The location was chosen for two reasons: it lies far from Central, and it barely suffered in the 3rd Civil War, so it kept a sizable educated population.

The laboratories answer to Chief Research Officer Gabriel Ivanov, and their great hope is unparalleled advances in robotics. What else they work on is known only to the Chief Officers. Rejuvenation, cybernetics and spaceflight are the usual guesses.
poiARC005-desc:
Every other division of the American Reclamation Corporation has a name you can print on a ration crate. The Seventh Division has only a number. Officially it is an office of strategic analytics and compliance that audits contracts, prices risk and advises the Board on foreign partnerships. Its reported value is modest, its offices are few, and almost nobody outside Arcopolis can name someone who works there.

The number is older than the division. During the mergers of the 2170s and '80s, Moderski's lawyers numbered each company in the ledgers before it was renamed. Acquisition 7 was a District insurance and census contractor. It was dull work, but it held something nobody else did: population records from before the Siege of Washington. Central lost most of its own archives in 2084. Acquisition 7 still knew who had lived where, who survived which flood, and who owed what to whom. Its old name was tied to a claims scandal, so ARC never gave it a new one. Inside the Corporation, it is simply called Seven. Its first asset was a memory, and it has kept adding to it ever since.

Its real work is simpler than its title. Each ARC delegation abroad, each shipping manifest, each hospital file and each checkpoint log ends up in the Seventh Division's archives. A trade deal tells ARC what a nation needs. A grain shipment tells it how hungry that nation is. A rejuvenation waitlist tells it which ministers want to live longer, and what they would give for it. Division 7 doesn't need spies. It has customers, and customers file paperwork.

What the Seventh Division does with all this is harder to pin down. Contracts in some countries turn out to have clauses nobody remembers agreeing to. Rival firms lose their suppliers the same week they make a bid. Some District councils that start asking whether the contract can be cancelled find their water allocations suddenly under review. Division 7 has never been caught doing any of it, and ARC is happy to point that out.

On paper, Seven answers to the Board. In practice it answers to Chief Financial Officer Suzanne Fielding, who already runs most of ARC on Moderski's behalf. It is how she keeps the Vice Presidents in line without spending any of her own capital. Its Director appears on no org chart and is known internally only as the Auditor. The oversight boards ARC appoints in the Districts are mostly left alone with their holidays and their augmentations. Seven has every receipt. Fielding just hasn't needed them yet, and a board that knows it is being watched stays obedient.

Its accounts are as quiet as its offices. On the books, Seven is a consultancy that sells risk assessments to foreign governments and partner firms. Nations pay ARC for analysis built from their own trade data, then make decisions ARC already saw coming. The rest of its costs are billed to other divisions: its surveillance to one, its field operations to another. If the true size of the Seventh Division were ever made public, it would rank among the largest parts of the Corporation. That is the main reason it never will be.

The Corporation says the Seventh Division just makes sure ARC is never surprised. Critics in Central call it the most dangerous intelligence service on the continent, the only one whose budget is paid by the people it watches.
